title: Education Becky Allen How Teaching Might Finally Learn
author: Allen, Becky
summary: Allen argues that the core problem in education improvement is not a shortage of instructional ideas -- AI has only multiplied those -- but a verification problem: we lack cheap, reliable ways to test which of many plausible instructional decisions actually produce better learning. Every instructional choice (splitting vs. inspection for factoring, planetary vs. energy-level model for atoms, sequential vs. comparative history teaching) is a wager on things we cannot directly observe, and the profession has been bad at discovering and preserving what works. Allen's conditional optimism is that LLM-supported online teaching may finally make it economically viable to test thousands of small instructional decisions at scale and gradually build a more cumulative science of how particular ideas are best taught. This is not an argument that LLMs possess pedagogical theory or that online testing reduces education to optimisation -- it is the modest claim that the economics of educational verification may be changing. Allen is careful to distinguish her position from naive enthusiasm: the verification problem is real and cannot be wished away with dashboards or bigger models.
points: * The deepest problem in education is not a shortage of instructional ideas but the verification problem: there is no cheap, reliable way to test which instructional decisions produce better learning rather than just better short-term performance. * Teaching has a memory problem compounding the verification problem: individual teachers discover countless things that work, but the profession is structurally bad at preserving that knowledge -- insights retire, move schools, or disappear with folders. * Assessment is a poor reward function for improving instruction: tests are sparse, delayed, and incomplete, and a system optimising what is easiest to measure may raise the signal while damaging the thing we actually care about. * LLM-supported online teaching may change the economics of educational verification: the ability to randomise instructional choices across many students and measure outcomes could make it cheap to test thousands of small decisions. * The limitation of school-level randomised trials is not that they are methodologically wrong but that they are too expensive and too coarse to test the granular instructional decisions that actually drive classroom learning.
quotes: The trouble with instruction is that it is cheap to propose and expensive to verify.

A teacher can propose pupils should be taught to factorise quadratics by splitting the middle term, whilst another says it is best to teach the inspection method of trying pairs of factors until they fit.

These decisions are wagers on things we cannot directly observe: whether pupils will come away with the firmer understanding, build a useful mental model or a misconception that will surface years later, grasp a pattern or merely memorise a label.

Teaching has a memory problem and a verification problem. Human teachers discover countless small things that work, but the profession is bad at preserving them. Machines, by contrast, may have perfect memory. They do not retire, forget, move schools, or lose a folder of carefully crafted lesson plans. But memory is not enough.
A system can only improve its teaching if it can tell when one instructional choice was better than another.

If a machine optimises whatever is easiest to measure, whether it is short-term accuracy or engagement, it may learn to raise the signal while damaging the thing we actually care about. It may learn to teach to the test in the most literal sense.

My optimism is merely that I think LLM-supported online teaching may finally make it cheap enough to test thousands of small instructional decisions, preserve what is learned, and gradually build a more cumulative science of how particular ideas are best taught.
